name: Handjass
description: Handjass, also known as Sackjass or Butzer, is considered the most basic and fundamental form of Jass, the national card game of Switzerland. It is a trick-taking game where players compete to reach a target score (usually represented by strokes on a slate) while avoiding the 'null' (potato) - a penalty for failing to reach a minimum point threshold in a hand.
deck: 36-card Swiss Jass deck (Roses, Bells, Acorns, Shields)

history.origins: Part of the extensive Jass family of games which have been popular in Switzerland since the late 18th century. Handjass is the 'direct' version of the game, simpler than the partnership-based Schieber.
timeline: 1790s: Earliest records of Jass games in Switzerland.
19th Century: Jass becomes the dominant card game in the country.
Present: Remains a staple of Swiss social life and pub culture.
history.cultural: Jass is so culturally significant in Switzerland that it is often referred to as the 'national sport' or the 'fourth language' of the country.
history.evolution: Handjass has remained relatively stable, though the threshold to avoid a 'null' has evolved from 21 points to 26 points in modern play to increase the challenge.

setup.deck: 36-card Jass deck (6-10, Jack, Queen, King, Ace). In German-speaking areas, the suits are Roses, Bells, Acorns and Shields. In French-speaking areas, standard French suits are used.
setup.dealing: Deal all cards (9 per player in a 4-player game). For 2-3 players, a 'blind hand' or 'besern' mechanic may be used.
setup.equipment: A slate or score sheet to mark 'strokes' (points).

rules.objective: Be the first player to reach a target number of strokes (e.g., 7 or 9) without falling below the minimum point threshold in any given hand.
rules.gameplay: 1. Players follow suit if possible. If they cannot follow suit, they may play any card (including a trump). 2. Trump Rules: In Jass, the 'Trump Under' (Jack) and 'Trump Nell' (Nine) are the highest cards. 3. A player may 'trump in' even if they can follow suit, unless they are playing the 'Jack of Trumps' (Pur). 4. Points are counted from cards taken in tricks.
keyRules: Trump Jack (Under) and Trump 9 (Nell) are the highest trumps.
Need at least 26 points to avoid a 'null' (penalty).

strategy.basic: Focus on taking at least 26 points to avoid the penalty. It is often better to dump high cards into an opponent's trick if you've already reached your threshold.
strategy.intermediate: Count the trumps carefully. Knowing when the 'Jack' and 'Nell' have been played is critical.
strategy.advanced: Tactical passing or leading: Decide whether to push for a match (100+ points) or play conservatively to simply guarantee your single stroke.
tips: Keep the Trump Under if possible; it is worth 20 points and nearly guarantees your threshold if you win the last trick.
In Berner Handjass, pay attention to the multipliers for specific suits.

scoring.description: Points from cards in tricks. Total 157 points per hand. 26-100 points = 1 stroke; over 100 = 2 strokes; under 26 = null (penalty).
scoring.winCondition: First player to reach target strokes (typically 7 or 9) wins.
